break_scenarios.title: Kotlin bootstrap closures allocated via raw malloc -- invisible to RC
break_scenarios.scenario: The Kotlin bootstrap (LlvmCodegen.kt line 1286) allocates closures with `call ptr @malloc(i64 ...)` + `nova_rt_track_raw`, which only bumps counters -- NO RC header is written. nova_rc_is_managed returns 0 for these pointers. Every nova_rc_inc and nova_rc_dec on a closure from the Kotlin-compiled path is a silent no-op. The design (Section 4.3) claims nova_rc_inc will be emitted for closure captures, and Section 5.2 claims nova_rc_dec at function exit will clean up closure slots. But both are no-ops because the pointer has no RC header. Every closure and every captured value it holds LEAKS. The self-hosted compiler (line 15278) correctly uses nova_rt_struct_alloc, so this is a Kotlin-vs-self-hosted divergence, but since the Kotlin bootstrap is still used for building the self-hosted compiler, and both compilers must pass the same oracle gates, the full RC design cannot be tested against the Kotlin-compiled binary until closures are migrated to nova_rt_struct_alloc.
break_scenarios.why_design_misses_it: Section 4.3 assumes closures are allocated via nova_heap_alloc with an RC header. It never audits the actual allocation path. The Kotlin bootstrap uses raw malloc for closures (line 1286), making ALL RC operations on closures no-ops. Section 12 (File Locations) lists LlvmCodegen.kt line 1266-1296 for closure changes, but the required change is not 'add capture-inc' -- it is 'change malloc to nova_rt_struct_alloc', which the design never mentions.

break_scenarios.title: nova_rc_free for CHANNEL does not dec buffered items -- every in-flight message leaks
break_scenarios.scenario: When a channel's RC reaches 0, nova_rc_free (line 7774-7784) does `free(ch->buf)` but does NOT iterate the buffered items and call nova_rc_dec_internal on each. Since channel_send deep-copies every value (creating fresh allocations with RC=1 owned solely by the buffer), freeing the buffer without decrementing those items leaks every value still sitting in the channel. This is acknowledged in the memory file as 'chan still ~2000' but the design document (Section 5.4) claims 'ALREADY HANDLED by the runtime' and lists the rc_free paths for LIST, DICT, STRUCT -- but never verifies the CHANNEL path. The channel rc_free explicitly does NOT dec buffered items.
break_scenarios.why_design_misses_it: Section 5.4 asserts 'ALREADY HANDLED by the runtime' and lists LIST/DICT/STRUCT rc_free paths but never checks the CHANNEL case. The actual nova_rc_free for NOVA_MEM_CHANNEL at line 7774 does only `free(ch->buf)` with no element iteration. Section 7 mentions channels in the context of deep-copy isolation but does not address their destructor's failure to release buffered values.

break_scenarios.title: slot_store dec-before-store on entry-block parameter initialization dec's a zero (performance), but with NOVA_T8_FULLRC the Kotlin bootstrap dec's on EVERY SlotStore including first store
break_scenarios.scenario: The existing Kotlin bootstrap (LlvmCodegen.kt line 627-634) already emits nova_rc_dec on EVERY slot store to rcSlots -- including the very first store in the entry block, which loads the zero-initialized value (0) and calls nova_rc_dec(0). While this is safe (nova_rc_dec early-returns for val < 0x10000), it is a wasted function call per slot per function. The design acknowledges this (Section 5.1 mentions 'skip the FIRST store in entry block') but the Kotlin bootstrap has NO such first-store tracking -- it dec's unconditionally. For a function with 20 heap-typed locals, that is 20 wasted calls to nova_rc_dec(0) on entry. At ~5ns each (pointer validation + early-return), this adds ~100ns per function call. For a recursive function like the compiler's own type inference (called millions of times), this is measurable. The self-hosted compiler design proposes adding entry_stores tracking, but the Kotlin bootstrap plan in Section 11 says 'near-no-op change' -- it is not a no-op, it requires adding per-slot first-store tracking logic that does not currently exist in the Kotlin codegen.
break_scenarios.why_design_misses_it: Section 5.1 correctly identifies the need to skip the first store but Section 11 (Implementation Checklist) for the Kotlin bootstrap says 'Modify: when NOVA_T8_FULLRC=1, ALL heap-typed slots are rcSlots ... This should be a near-no-op change since rcSlots already captures most heap slots'. This handwaves over the missing first-store-skip logic. The Kotlin codegen has no concept of entry-block-first-store tracking.

break_scenarios.title: field_get borrow used across a mutating call -- container mutation invalidates borrow, then caller reads freed memory
break_scenarios.scenario: The design (Section 3) says field_get/index_get results are BORROWED and require zero RC if used only transiently (passed to a call, never stored). But a 'transient' borrow can span a call that mutates the source container. If the call causes the container to be reallocated or the element to be replaced, the borrowed pointer is invalidated. nova_rt_list_set dec's the old element (line 1107), which may free it if RC=1. The caller's register still holds the pointer to the freed value. This is the classic iterator-invalidation bug. The borrow elision (Section 3) explicitly states 'The container holding the value keeps RC >= 1 for the entire expression' -- but 'expression' is wrong; the borrow lives across an arbitrary call that can mutate the container.
break_scenarios.minimal_repro:
fn process(lst)
  let val = lst[0]        // field_get -> borrowed, no rc_inc
  lst[0] = "new_value"    // nova_rt_list_set: rc_dec(old), rc_inc(new)
                           // old is the value 'val' points to. If RC was 1, it is freed.
  print(val)               // USE-AFTER-FREE: val points to freed memory

let items = ["hello"]
process(items)
break_scenarios.why_design_misses_it: Section 3 defines borrow safety as 'The container holding the value keeps RC >= 1 for the entire expression.' But the borrow extends beyond the expression -- `val` is loaded from the list, then a SEPARATE statement mutates the list (replacing index 0), then a THIRD statement uses val. The borrow lifetime spans multiple statements. The design's 'transient borrow' elision rule says elide if 'ONLY used as an argument to a call' -- but the NOVA IR would store the index_get result into a slot (since it is used later), which triggers rule 4.1 (slot_store of alias -> rc_inc). So the design would actually insert rc_inc here IF the slot_store of the index_get result is recognized as an alias store. The question is: does ire_borrow_src correctly mark the index_get result as non-owned, causing the slot_store to emit rc_inc? The self-hosted compiler at line 15129 sets ire_borrow_src[dest] = 1, but this is described as 'inert metadata' -- it is NOT read by any insertion logic in the current design. The design says 'not in ire_owned' triggers rc_inc at slot_store (Section 4.1), and index_get results are not in ire_owned, so the inc WOULD be emitted. But this depends on Stage C being implemented, not Stage A. Stages A and B alone do NOT emit rc_inc -- they only add decs. So between Stage A and Stage C, there is a window where the borrow is unprotected.

break_scenarios.title: Double-dec when a returned value's source slot is ALSO dec'd at function exit due to imprecise load_origin tracking
break_scenarios.scenario: Section 5.2 says 'the returned value's source slot is EXCLUDED from cleanup dec' and Section 4.5 says 'nova_rc_inc before cleanup'. The design relies on ire_load_origin to identify which slot the return value came from. But ire_load_origin tracks only the LAST load_origin set for a register. If the return value goes through a copy or phi-like merge (e.g., return from inside an if-else where both branches load from different slots), the load_origin may not be set, or may point to the wrong slot. In that case, the returned-slot exclusion fails: the inc fires (Section 4.5), and the slot is also dec'd at cleanup (Section 5.2). If the returned value and the slot point to the same object, this is balanced (inc + dec = net zero, plus the caller's ownership). But if load_origin is WRONG (points to slot A when the value actually came from slot B), slot A is excluded from cleanup (leaked), and slot B is dec'd (possibly freeing the returned value). The caller then holds a dangling pointer.
break_scenarios.why_design_misses_it: The design stages A and B before C. During the Stage A+B window, slot_store overwrites emit dec (Stage A) but NO inc (Stage C not yet active). So storing a parameter value into a local slot (result = a) does not increment RC. At function exit, the local slot 'result' is dec'd (it is not a param, not excluded). The parameter slot 'a' is excluded (it is a param). But result and a point to the same object. The dec on result drops RC to 0 (the object was RC=1 from the caller's ownership). The caller's slot now holds a freed object. This is a use-after-free that exists during the Stage A+B window before Stage C closes it. The design claims Stages A+B are 'conservative (they only add dec operations, never inc)' and 'A missing dec is a leak (benign), not a UAF'. This is WRONG. Adding dec without the corresponding inc creates UAF.

break_scenarios.title: Stages A+B without C: dec without inc is UAF, not 'benign leak'
break_scenarios.scenario: The design (end of Section 9, Stage C rationale) claims 'Stages A and B are CONSERVATIVE (they only add dec operations, never inc). A missing dec is a leak (benign), not a UAF.' This is the fundamental error in the staged rollout. A dec WITHOUT a corresponding inc means the RC under-represents the actual reference count. When a value is aliased (loaded from one slot, stored into another), the second slot's dec at function exit decrements RC without any prior inc. If the first slot was already cleaned up (or is a parameter), the RC hits 0 prematurely. The object is freed while the second slot or the caller still references it. This is exactly the failure mode that caused 33 use-after-free crashes in the previous attempt (mentioned in Section 0). Adding ONLY decs is strictly more dangerous than adding ONLY incs (which would leak, not crash).
break_scenarios.why_design_misses_it: Section 9 Stage C rationale explicitly states the assumption that stages A+B alone are safe because 'they only add dec operations'. This directly contradicts the RC invariant in Section 1: 'every operation that CREATES a new reference emits nova_rc_inc'. Omitting the inc while adding the dec violates the invariant. The previous failed attempt (Section 0: '33 use-after-free crashes') was exactly this: 'Aggressive drop without counting'. Stages A+B without C repeat this same mistake with different framing.

break_scenarios.title: nova_rc_is_managed pointer validation is O(1) amortized but has high constant factor -- ~30-50ns per call
break_scenarios.scenario: Every nova_rc_inc and nova_rc_dec calls nova_rc_is_managed (line 7841/7864), which calls nova_mem_find_tag (line 7829). nova_mem_find_tag performs: null check, range check against [heap_base,heap_top), alignment check (addr & 7), IsBadReadPtr (Windows-only, involves kernel call on each probe), RC header magic validation (read at ptr-4), RC >= 1 check (read at ptr-8), and for LIST/DICT/CHANNEL kinds, structural validation (reading size/cap fields deep into the object). On Windows, IsBadReadPtr is a system call that costs ~100-500ns. Even on Linux, the header reads (ptr-4, ptr-8) are cold cache misses for objects not recently accessed. The design (Section 6) estimates '~5ns each via the nova_mem_find_tag fast-path'. This is wildly optimistic. The fast-path early-exits are only for non-heap values (< 0x10000). For actual heap objects, the full validation runs. With full RC, EVERY slot store overwrite and EVERY function-exit cleanup triggers this validation for each heap-typed slot.
break_scenarios.why_design_misses_it: Section 6 estimates '~5ns each via the nova_mem_find_tag fast-path = ~0.5-1.0 microsecond total'. The fast-path (val < 0x10000) only fires for non-heap values. For heap objects -- the ONLY case where RC operations matter -- the FULL validation path runs. On Windows, IsBadReadPtr alone costs ~100ns. The design never benchmarks the actual cost of nova_mem_find_tag on a real heap pointer.

break_scenarios.title: Atomic RC on EVERY carrier thread even when values never cross threads
break_scenarios.scenario: nova_is_multithreaded is set to 1 as soon as ANY spawn occurs (line 5506, 6274). Once set, it is NEVER unset. Every subsequent nova_rc_inc and nova_rc_dec uses InterlockedIncrement/InterlockedDecrement (atomic RMW) for ALL values on ALL threads, including values that are thread-local and never shared. With the M:N scheduler, spawning 10k green tasks sets nova_is_multithreaded = 1 permanently. The deep-copy isolation model means values are NEVER shared between tasks, yet every RC operation pays the atomic cost (~15-25ns on x86 vs ~1-3ns for non-atomic increment). The design (Section 8) says 'no interaction' with the M:N scheduler and 'Green tasks on the same carrier thread share a single OS thread, so their RC operations are non-contending.' Non-contending atomics are STILL slower than non-atomic operations: InterlockedIncrement requires a LOCK prefix that forces cache-line exclusivity, even if uncontended.
break_scenarios.why_design_misses_it: Section 8 'Interaction with M:N scheduler' says 'no interaction' and claims green tasks on the same carrier share RC operations without contention. This is true but irrelevant: the issue is that nova_is_multithreaded is a GLOBAL flag that once set, forces ALL RC to be atomic on ALL threads, including the main thread after all spawned tasks have completed. The design never proposes per-thread or per-value atomic tracking.

break_scenarios.title: Self-referencing dict cycle leaks unboundedly in a long-running server with no v1 mitigation
break_scenarios.scenario: Section 7 acknowledges cycles and says 'accept-and-bound for v1'. The 'bound' argument is 'Most NOVA programs create tree-shaped data'. The mitigation is 'Per-request arenas (future)'. But per-request arenas are listed as 'future' -- they do not exist. The weak() function exists but the design acknowledges developers must 'knowingly create cyclic structures' to use it. The problem is that COMMON patterns create cycles WITHOUT the developer knowing: a struct with a dict field where the dict gets a backreference (ORM-style parent/child), or a closure capturing a variable that contains the closure (event handlers). In a web server handling 100k req/s, even 1 cycle per 1000 requests = 100 leaked objects/second = 8.6M leaked objects/day. The design's own problem statement says this is the exact issue: 'After 1M requests the process consumes gigabytes of unreachable memory.' Moving from 16k leaks/request to 1 cycle-leak/request is progress but does not achieve 'flat memory' for a server running for days.
break_scenarios.why_design_misses_it: Section 7 says 'Most NOVA programs create tree-shaped data' and 'cycles require deliberate construction'. But closure captures + dict mutation is an EXTREMELY common pattern (event handlers, middleware chains, request context objects). The design acknowledges cycles are possible but provides NO v1 mitigation that is actually implemented. weak() requires developer awareness. Per-request arenas are 'future'. Arena mode (NOVA_AUTO_ARENA=1) is a whole-program bypass that eliminates ALL deterministic freeing. The framework readiness target (forge server with flat memory) CANNOT be met if any handler creates even one cycle per request.

break_scenarios.title: Global slots excluded from RC entirely -- module-level mutable state leaks on every overwrite
break_scenarios.scenario: The Kotlin bootstrap (LlvmCodegen.kt line 627) explicitly excludes global slots from RC operations: `if (!inst.slot.isGlobal && inst.slot.name in rcSlots && !bothScalar)`. The condition requires `!inst.slot.isGlobal` -- so stores to global slots NEVER emit rc_dec on the old value and NEVER emit rc_inc for aliases. Module-level variables that hold heap values and are reassigned will leak the old value on every overwrite. The self-hosted compiler's slot_store handler (line 14820-14831) also operates on `%slot.<value>` where `value` comes from the IR, but the design document Section 5.1 never addresses global slots. The proposed implementation in Section 11 says 'replace the Stage 3 conditional block' but does not add a global-slot path.
break_scenarios.why_design_misses_it: Section 5.1 says 'A heap-typed slot %slot.X is being overwritten with a new value' but never distinguishes local from global slots. The Kotlin bootstrap explicitly gates RC on `!inst.slot.isGlobal`. The design's implementation checklist (Section 11) instructs modifying the slot_store handler but does not address the global-slot exclusion. Global slot RC requires different treatment (no function-exit cleanup since the slot outlives the function; only overwrite-dec + alias-inc).

break_scenarios.title: nova_rt_list_pop returns without rc_dec -- under full RC the popped element's RC is permanently inflated by 1
break_scenarios.scenario: nova_rt_list_append calls nova_rc_inc(elem) when inserting (line 1017). nova_rt_list_pop (line 1118-1126) removes the last element and returns it WITHOUT calling nova_rc_dec. The comment says 'Ownership TRANSFERS to the caller (NO rc_dec)'. Under the current partial-RC model this makes sense: the list's inc is 'transferred' to the caller. But under full RC (Section 2 calling convention), the CALLER borrows the returned value and will handle it. The issue: the element was rc_inc'd on append, and on pop it is NOT rc_dec'd. The caller receives an owned reference (RC stays at the append-incremented level). When the caller's slot is cleaned up, rc_dec fires and brings RC to 0 -- IF the caller is the only other reference. But if the element was originally put in with rc_inc (so RC went from 1 to 2 on append), and pop does not dec (RC stays 2), and the caller's cleanup decs (RC goes to 1), the element is NEVER freed because RC=1, not 0. The original allocator's reference was already cleaned up. Wait -- actually the design's convention says: the list_append rc_inc'd the element, making the list an owner. Pop transfers ownership from the list to the caller. The list no longer holds a reference. If pop does not dec, the RC correctly represents the transfer (one less owner: list, one new owner: caller). So the count stays the same. This is actually CORRECT for the 'transfer ownership' semantic. Let me re-examine... Actually, the element's RC was incremented by list_append (from 1 to 2 if the original slot still exists). Pop does not dec (RC stays 2). The original slot's cleanup will dec (RC goes to 1). The caller's slot cleanup will dec (RC goes to 0). This is correct. The leak only happens if the original creating slot was ALREADY cleaned up before pop, making the list the sole owner (RC=1). Pop transfers to caller (RC still 1, correct). Caller dec's (RC=0, freed). OK this is actually sound. Let me instead focus on the ACTUAL list_pop soundness issue: list_pop returns `nova_rt_unbox_elem(value)` which for boxed floats KEEPS the box (returns the same pointer). So the pop transfers the box's reference to the caller. For bools, it returns `bx->payload` (raw 0/1), discarding the box. The box is still in the list's now-decremented-size area (logically removed but the data array still holds the pointer). On list free, the data array is freed but elements beyond size are not dec'd. The bool box leaks. Actually no -- list_pop decrements `list->size` (line 1124 `--list->size`), so the element at the old last position is no longer in the logical list. When the list is freed via nova_rc_free, it iterates `i < l->size` and does not visit the popped slot. So the popped element is not dec'd by the list destructor. For a bool box, unbox_elem returns raw 0/1, and the original box pointer is abandoned -- neither the caller (who got raw 0/1) nor the list destructor (which won't visit it) will dec it. The box leaks. This is a real leak but minor.
break_scenarios.minimal_repro:
let lst = []
let i = 0
while i < 100000
  push(lst, true)  // true -> nova_rt_box_bool -> box with RC=1, list_append rc_inc -> RC=2
  let v = pop(lst)  // unbox_elem returns raw 0/1, box pointer abandoned. RC=2, no dec.
  i = i + 1
// 100k leaked bool boxes (each 16 bytes + 8 byte RC header = 24 bytes = ~2.4 MB)
break_scenarios.why_design_misses_it: Section 5.4 says 'ALREADY HANDLED by the runtime' for container element removal and lists list_set (which dec's old element). But list_pop is not analyzed. The pop-unbox interaction (unbox discards the box for bools, abandoning the RC reference) is a novel leak vector not covered by any section of the design.

break_scenarios.title: Staged rollout allows Stages A+B to ship a UAF-introducing change gated only by an env var -- no compile-time safety
break_scenarios.scenario: The design proposes that NOVA_T8_FULLRC=1 activates Stages A through G progressively. But the ASAN gate (Section 9) runs the FULL test suite only at each stage boundary. Between stages, a developer or CI system with NOVA_T8_FULLRC=1 gets whatever stage was last committed. If Stage A+B is committed without Stage C, any program that aliases a value between slots will UAF (as described in the 'Stages A+B without C' scenario). The env var NOVA_T8_FULLRC does not have sub-stage granularity (no NOVA_T8_FULLRC_STAGE=A/B/C). So there is no way to get 'only Stage A' or 'only Stage A+B' behavior -- the flag enables whatever code was compiled in. This means the staged rollout is actually an ALL-OR-NOTHING deployment: all stages must be committed together, or the intermediate states are unsound.
break_scenarios.why_design_misses_it: Section 9 Stage C rationale says 'Stages A and B are CONSERVATIVE (they only add dec operations, never inc). A missing dec is a leak (benign), not a UAF.' This claim is mathematically wrong. Adding dec without corresponding inc means RC under-counts actual references. Under-counting causes premature free, which is UAF, not a leak. The staged rollout creates a window of unsoundness between each stage.

overall_verdict:
The design has TWO fatal flaws and should NOT be implemented as staged.

FATAL FLAW #1: The staged rollout (A+B before C) is fundamentally unsound. The design claims adding only decs (Stages A+B) without adding incs (Stage C) is 'conservative' and causes only 'benign leaks'. This is backwards. Adding decs without incs UNDER-COUNTS references, causing premature free (UAF), not leaks. OVER-counting (adding incs without decs) would cause leaks. This is the exact same mistake that caused 33 UAFs in the previous attempt (Section 0). Stages A+B+C+D MUST be deployed atomically as a single commit, or not at all. The inc and dec are two halves of the same invariant -- splitting them across stages violates the invariant in the intermediate state.

FATAL FLAW #2: The channel destructor (nova_rc_free for NOVA_MEM_CHANNEL) does not dec buffered items. Under full RC, this means every value sitting in a channel buffer when the channel is freed becomes a permanent leak. Combined with the cycle problem (closures capturing dicts that reference the closures), this makes the design unable to achieve its stated goal of 'flat memory for a production server'. The design's Section 5.4 claims channel cleanup is 'ALREADY HANDLED' -- it is not.

Beyond the fatal flaws: the Kotlin bootstrap allocates closures via raw malloc (no RC header), making all RC operations on closures silent no-ops; global slots are excluded from RC entirely; the nova_mem_find_tag validation cost is dramatically underestimated (~30-50ns on heap objects, not ~5ns); and the atomic-RC-everywhere-after-first-spawn penalty is never addressed.

The design IS sound in its theoretical invariant (Section 13's formal argument is correct IF all stages are deployed simultaneously). The implementation plan is where it breaks. Recommendation: merge Stages A+B+C+D into a single atomic stage; fix the channel destructor; fix the Kotlin bootstrap closure allocation; add global-slot RC handling; and benchmark nova_mem_find_tag on real heap pointers before committing to the performance estimates.
